summary: English version of the Greek half of Ashoka's 1958 bilingual at Kandahar, which renders dharma as eusebeia ('Piety'); the Aramaic half, in the same entry, says 'our lord, king Pridarsh, became the institutor of Truth'.
limits: Wikipedia reproduces translations and the Greek text without a stated edition; the Aramaic half has '(?)' marks for doubtful readings and is not an exact translation of the Greek. The entry's account of Kosambi's claim of two independent renderings was not verified.

text.edition: Wikipedia 'Kandahar Bilingual Rock Inscription': Greek by G. P. Carratelli; Aramaic after Sircar, Asokan Studies p. 115

composition.basis: Wikipedia says c. 260 BCE, in about the 8th year of the reign; Sircar reads 'ten years having elapsed since his coronation'.

text.witness: Rock inscription at Chil Zena, Kandahar, found 1958 (Scerrato); the stone is the witness.

strand.to: Greek and Aramaic-reading Iranian subjects at Kandahar
strand.what: dharma translated as eusebeia and as 'Truth' (Aramaic)

title: Kandahar Greek Edicts of Ashoka (Wheeler translation, Schlumberger Greek)
venue: Wikipedia; translation by R. E. M. Wheeler, Greek text by D. Schlumberger (CRAI 1964)
ask_addressed: Quote the primary evidence for Indo-Iranian and Indian contact: the Hittite-Mitanni treaty (c. 1380 BCE) invoking Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas; the Rigveda (hymns to Indra, Mitra-Varuna) in an opened translation; Yasna 30 from the Avesta; the Edicts of Ashoka (Rock Edict 13 naming Greek kings; the Greek and Aramaic inscriptions at Kandahar); the Behistun inscription.
quote: he conquered Kalinga. A hundred and fifty thousand persons were captured and deported
summary: Wheeler's translation of the Old Kandahar plaque: the Greek of the end of RE XII and the start of RE XIII, naming the king 'Piodasses'; the entry takes it as showing Mauryan control of Arachosia.
limits: Secondary host; Schlumberger's Greek (cited as CRAI 108, 1964, doi 10.3406/crai.1964.11695) was not opened beyond the abstract page, which does not carry the text. The 'control of Arachosia' inference is Dupree's via the entry.

title: Behistun, Persian Text: column I, paragraph 6 (the lands of Darius)
venue: Livius.org (adapted King/Thompson translation of the Old Persian text)
ask_addressed: Quote the primary evidence for Indo-Iranian and Indian contact: the Hittite-Mitanni treaty (c. 1380 BCE) invoking Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas; the Rigveda (hymns to Indra, Mitra-Varuna) in an opened translation; Yasna 30 from the Avesta; the Edicts of Ashoka (Rock Edict 13 naming Greek kings; the Greek and Aramaic inscriptions at Kandahar); the Behistun inscription.
quote: Drangiana , Aria , Chorasmia , Bactria , Sogdia , Gandara , Scythia , Sattagydia , Arachosia and Maka ; twenty-three lands in all
summary: Darius's list of 23 subject lands, with the eastern ones Aria, Bactria, Gandara, Sattagydia and Arachosia, the borderland where Persian, Greek and Mauryan power later met at Kandahar.
limits: Livius's adapted older translation; the page's spacing before commas is kept. The passage names Gandara but no Indian ruler; no contact with Mauryan India is stated.

title: Behistun, Persian Text: column IV, paragraph 70 ('Aryan script')
venue: Livius.org (adapted King/Thompson translation of the Old Persian text)
ask_addressed: Quote the primary evidence for Indo-Iranian and Indian contact: the Hittite-Mitanni treaty (c. 1380 BCE) invoking Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas; the Rigveda (hymns to Indra, Mitra-Varuna) in an opened translation; Yasna 30 from the Avesta; the Edicts of Ashoka (Rock Edict 13 naming Greek kings; the Greek and Aramaic inscriptions at Kandahar); the Behistun inscription.
quote: Besides, it was in Aryan script , and it was composed on clay tablets and on parchment
summary: Darius calls his own writing 'Aryan' and says the text was sent out across the provinces, a self-use of 'Aryan' for the Iranian world relevant to the Indo-Iranian ethnonym.
limits: Translation's word 'Aryan' stands for Old Persian ariya; the page does not discuss the term or any Indian use. The page spacing before commas is kept.
